questions.question: What does a 'search model' (e.g., triangle search model) treat figure counting as?
options: A systematic search through all possible combinations of points/lines to find every valid instance of the target shape
A purely visual guessing exercise
A random sampling process
A process with no defined stopping point
questions.rationale: A search model treats figure counting as systematically searching through all possible point/line combinations to find every valid instance of the target shape.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a 'coordinate model' in figure counting?
options: To avoid using any numbers
To only measure the figure's color intensity
Assigning coordinates to each vertex so figures can be validated mathematically (e.g., checking collinearity or area) rather than just visually
To replace the need for labeling vertices
questions.rationale: A coordinate model assigns numeric coordinates to vertices, enabling mathematical validation (like checking for collinearity or computing area) instead of relying purely on visual judgment.

questions.question: How can 'triangle area validation' using coordinates help confirm a candidate triangle is genuinely valid?
options: It can't help — area is irrelevant to validity
If the computed area from the three points' coordinates is zero, the points are collinear and don't actually form a triangle
A zero area always means the triangle is valid
Area validation only works for right triangles
questions.rationale: If three points are collinear (lie on the same straight line), the area formula computed from their coordinates evaluates to zero, revealing that they don't actually form a valid triangle.

questions.question: What does 'figure counting as search' emphasize about the counting process?
options: That it cannot be automated in any way
That counting is unrelated to combinatorics
That only one candidate figure ever needs to be checked
That it can be treated as generating all valid candidate combinations and then filtering out the invalid ones, similar to a search algorithm
questions.rationale: This framing treats figure counting like a search algorithm: generate all candidate combinations, then filter out the ones that don't actually form valid figures.

questions.question: What is 'candidate generation' in this search-based approach?
options: Producing every possible combination of points/segments that could potentially form a valid figure, before checking which ones actually are valid
Deleting all but one figure
Only generating triangles, never other shapes
Randomly generating a single candidate and stopping
questions.rationale: Candidate generation produces every possible combination that could plausibly form the target figure type, which is then filtered down through validation.

questions.question: What is 'deduplication' needed for in candidate generation?
options: It isn't actually needed
Only removing invalid figures
Removing candidates that represent the exact same figure counted more than once, which can happen when different generation orders produce the same shape
Sorting candidates alphabetically
questions.rationale: Deduplication removes cases where the same actual figure was generated more than once (e.g., via different starting points), preventing it from being double-counted.

questions.question: What does 'direction independence' mean when checking for duplicate figures?
options: Direction never matters for figures
The same figure found by tracing its boundary in different directions (e.g., clockwise vs anticlockwise) should still be recognized as one single figure, not two
Every direction produces a genuinely different figure
Only clockwise-traced figures are valid
questions.rationale: A figure traced clockwise and the same figure traced anticlockwise are still just one figure — direction independence ensures these aren't mistakenly counted as two separate figures.

questions.question: How can symmetry provide a 'shortcut' in figure counting?
options: Symmetry never helps with counting
Counting figures in one symmetric section of a figure and then multiplying or reflecting that count, instead of manually counting the entire figure
By eliminating the need to count squares
By doubling every count automatically regardless of the figure
questions.rationale: If a figure has symmetry, counting figures in just one symmetric section and then appropriately multiplying/reflecting that count can save significant time over counting the whole figure manually.

questions.question: What is the 'symmetry trap'?
options: Symmetric figures are always duplicates
Assuming two figures are duplicates just because they look symmetric to each other, when they may actually be distinct valid figures in different positions
Symmetric figures should never be counted
A trap that only applies to circles
questions.rationale: The symmetry trap is mistakenly treating two visually symmetric figures as duplicates and discarding one, when they are actually two distinct, separately valid figures in different positions.

questions.question: In a standard 3x3 square grid practice example, what is the total number of squares of all sizes?
questions.rationale: Using the earlier formula: 3^2 + 2^2 + 1^2 = 9 + 4 + 1 = 14 total squares.
